subject: physics
title: Energy, Damping and Resonance
welcome_lead: Trade kinetic for potential energy in an oscillator, then watch damping eat the amplitude.
meta_desc: A-Level Further Mechanics adventure on energy in SHM, damping and resonance.
final_note: Drive a lightly damped system at its natural frequency and you'll get resonance.

walkthroughs.body_html: At equilibrium: all KE. At amplitude: all PE. Total energy E = ½ k A² stays constant in an ideal oscillator. KE + PE = constant.
Light damping: amplitude decays exponentially. Heavy damping: very slow return to equilibrium, no oscillation. Critical damping: fastest return without overshoot.
When driving frequency equals natural frequency, amplitude grows large. Less damping = sharper, taller resonance peak. Examples: tuning forks, bridges, AC circuits.

mcqs.q: When energy is 'lost' as heat due to friction, what has really happened?
options: Energy has been converted into mass following E=mc^2.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
Energy has been transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings — it's not destroyed, just dissipated.
Energy has been used up and no longer exists.

mcqs.q: If a car doubles its speed, what happens to its kinetic energy?
options: No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
Kinetic energy doubles because energy is proportional to speed.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
It quadruples (because KE = 1/2 mv^2 — kinetic energy is proportional to v^2).

mcqs.q: Is the internal energy of a system the same as the heat it contains?
options: Yes — internal energy is just the stored heat in the object.
No — a system doesn't 'contain heat'; internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of its particles, changed by heating or doing work.
No — internal energy refers only to the chemical potential energy.
Kinetic energy stays the same because mass hasn't changed.
